title: Reset after a miss
summary: A short routine for the seconds after a lost target: five steps in 5–10 seconds, then the next target. The “why” waits until after the round.

body.html: A miss is over the moment the shot is fired; only the next target can still change. A short, fixed reset helps you leave the miss behind and start the next routine.

html: Gun safe: handle it as the rules require, muzzles in a safe direction.
One correction in two or three words, for example “stay on the line”.
A quick picture in your head of the right shot.

body.html: The reset has to fit the time limit. In Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ you have at most 15 seconds between singles or between doubles. In Compak® Sporting you have at most 10 seconds to call, counted from the shot at the previous station's target.
Save the “why” for after the round. Analysing a skill step by step under pressure can disrupt it, so on the stand keep to one short correction.
In Sporting™ the rules ask you to check your score on the card when you leave the stand (Chapter 16 · Recording results and checking your score).
Once you know the score of a stand, let it go: that stand is closed, and your attention belongs to the next one.

The same reset works after a referee decision you dislike. If you disagree, make a protest at once and in the correct way, then let it go once the decision is final. More in Warnings, cards and penalties.

html.sporting: Protest at once on the stand: raise a hand and say “appeal” or “protest” (Chapter 9 · How to protest on the stand). After the final decision you must shoot again within 15 seconds (Chapter 10 · Resume shooting within 15 seconds).
html.compak: Protest at once, before the next shooter calls: raise an arm and say “protest” or “appeal” (Chapter 19 · How to protest a referee's call). After the final decision you must resume within 10 seconds (Chapter 21 · Refusal to comply: 10 seconds to resume).

body.html: Going on arguing after a final decision counts as an attempt to influence the referee and can be penalised (Chapter 11 · What counts as influencing the referee, Chapter 22 · What counts as an attempt to influence).
A bad stand is not a bad day. Some shooters lose points early from nerves and shoot well once they settle; coaches often advise judging the day at the end, not after one stand.

notes.html: When your child misses, stay calm and quiet on the side. A calm face helps more than advice, and advice from behind the stand can count as coaching.
After a miss, do not translate comments or analysis unless the shooter asks. During a competition, pass on only the referee's decisions and official messages.
In training, practise the reset on purpose: after a missed target, ask the shooter to say the five steps aloud, then do them in silence.

key_points.html: Reset in 5–10 seconds: gun safe, breath out, one correction, one picture, next routine.
Ask “why” after the round, not on the stand.
After a referee decision: protest at once and correctly, then let it go.
A bad stand is not a bad day.

did_you_know.html: In a study of tenpin bowlers, a short routine after each throw also helped, and players felt it protected their focus.

quiz.q: What is the first step of the reset after a miss?

options.text: Work out exactly why you missed
Count up your score for the round so far
Make the gun safe, as the rules say

quiz.explain: Safety comes first; then one breath out, one correction, one picture and the next routine.

quiz.q: When is a good time to analyse why you missed?
quiz.explain: Step-by-step analysis on the stand can disrupt your shooting; one short correction is enough there.

quiz.q: You disagree with a referee's “zero”. What do you do?

options.text: Protest at once, then let it go
Complain to the squad after the round

quiz.explain: Protest at once in the correct way; once the decision is final, arguing on counts as an attempt to influence the referee.
